question: The Commission is considering introducing a uniform EU age limit for access to social media, citing the recommendations of an expert panel it has set up. Protecting children online is essential; however, the views of academics on the impact of social media, appropriate age limits and the role of parental control remain divided.

Member States have differing experiences, education systems and approaches to parents’ rights and responsibilities. Setting a single age limit across the EU is not merely a technical issue concerning the functioning of the internal market, but direct interference in decisions regarding the upbringing of children. In light of the above: 1.
Why does the Commission consider the recommendations of a single panel of experts to be a sufficient basis for proposing a uniform age limit across the EU?

How does the Commission intend to take into account the experiences of Member States, the principle of subsidiarity and the fundamental responsibility of parents for decisions regarding their children’s use of social media?

On what legal basis does the Commission intend to harmonise the age limit, and does it consider Article 114 TFEU to be appropriate for regulating a matter that goes beyond the removal of barriers to the internal market?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (6.10.2026) The co-chairs of the special panel on child safety online1 presented their report to the Commission on 13 July 2026.

The panel provided independent expert input on the EU’s child safety framework, with invitees from fields including health, neuroscience, psychology, computer science, child rights and digital literacy, as well as representatives from parent and family organisations. To ensure diverse perspectives, invited experts varied between each meeting of the special panel.

This broad expertise allowed the co-chairs to present balanced, in-depth and robust recommendations. The Commission considered these recommendations alongside all available data and evidence, including experience at national level across Member States.

It took account of the European Parliament’s report on the protection of minors online, which called for a harmonised European approach to minimum ages for access to social media2. It also considered the growing number of Member States that are introducing, or considering, national legislation establishing a minimum age for minors to access certain online services.

Against this background, the Commission remains mindful that divergent national approaches may increase compliance costs for companies operating across the EU. To avoid such fragmentation, the proposal for the EU KIDS Act3, which sets a harmonised EU approach for gradual exposure to autonomous social media use for minors, was adopted on the legal basis of Article 114 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU.
The Commission recognises the important role that parents play in keeping children safe online, as outlined in the guidelines on the protection of minors4 under the Digital Services Act5.

The essential role of parents is furthermore emphasised in the report of the special panel and forms a key tenet of the EU KIDS Act which permits parents to set up accounts for minors above 13 with limited age-appropriate features and parental controls.
1 https://commission.europa.eu/topics/digital-economy-and-society/special-panel_en. 2 European Parliament resolution of 26 November 2025 on the protection of minors online (2025/2060(INI)),
